oneSentence: The maximum amount of input and prior output a language model can use at one time while producing the next part of a response.
plainExplanation:
A language model works from a limited text buffer. That buffer holds the current instructions, the conversation so far, and often the model’s own recent reply. People often call this the context window or context length. Context limit usually means the maximum size allowed. Memory limit is ambiguous and should not be treated as a precise synonym.

What goes in? Usually the system instructions, your prompt, any pasted documents, and sometimes images or other data converted into model-readable pieces. These pieces are often counted as tokens, which are small chunks of text such as words, parts of words, or punctuation.

What happens? The model reads only the material that fits inside that limit and uses it to predict the next token. If the conversation or document is too long, some content may be cut off, summarised, or replaced, depending on the tool. Content outside the window is not available to the model at that moment unless the system adds it back.

What comes out? A response based on the material inside the current window, not on everything ever said. This is why a model may lose track of earlier details in a long exchange. It is also why a larger context window can help with long documents, but does not by itself give reliable long-term memory or better truthfulness.

everydayAnalogy.title: Only the pages open on the desk
everydayAnalogy.story: Amina and Luis are comparing two paragraphs that say the same thing in different words. They have many printed pages, but their desk is small, so only a few pages can stay open at once. When they need new pages, they remove some older ones from the desk and bring others in. Their comparison can use what is visible on the desk now, not every page they brought to the room.

mapping.aiElement: the tokens currently available to the model

mapping.analogyElement: removing older pages to make space
mapping.aiElement: dropping or truncating earlier content when the limit is reached
generating the next output using only the current context

everydayAnalogy.limitation: People can form durable memories, choose what to reread, and understand meaning in ways a model does not necessarily do. A context window is only a temporary input limit, usually measured in tokens, and it does not work like a human working memory.

visual.title: What fits inside the context window
visual.learningObjective: After using this explainer, a reader should be able to say what counts toward the context window, what happens when it fills up, and why this is not the same as long-term memory.
visual.description: An interactive panel shows a fixed-size window measured in tokens. Coloured segments represent system instructions, user text, document excerpts, and generated reply tokens. As the reader adds text, the bar fills. When the limit is exceeded, the oldest content fades out or is summarised, and the visible response changes accordingly.

steps.label: Start with an empty window
steps.explanation: The model begins with a fixed amount of space for the current task.
steps.visualInstruction: Show an empty horizontal token bar with a labelled maximum, such as 100 tokens.

steps.label: Add instructions and user text
steps.explanation: System instructions and the user’s prompt both take space before the answer starts.
steps.visualInstruction: Insert two coloured segments into the bar: one for system prompt, one for user prompt; display token counts beside each.

steps.label: Generate a reply
steps.explanation: The model’s own output also uses space, because later words can depend on earlier words in the same answer.
steps.visualInstruction: Animate reply tokens appearing as a third colour and shrinking the remaining free space counter.

steps.label: Exceed the limit
steps.explanation: When too much text is added, earlier material no longer fits unless the tool removes, compresses, or replaces something.
steps.visualInstruction: Let the reader drag in a long document segment; once over the limit, push the oldest segment out of view or swap it for a smaller summary block.

steps.label: Compare outcomes
steps.explanation: Different visible context can lead to different answers, even when the topic is the same.
steps.visualInstruction: Show two side-by-side responses: one with the earlier detail still present, one after it has been dropped.

visual.interaction: The reader can add or remove chunks of text, drag a slider for window size, and toggle whether overflow is truncated or summarised.
visual.accessibilityDescription: Screen-reader version: A narrated simulation describes a model with a fixed token budget. First, system instructions use part of the budget. Next, the user prompt uses more. Then the model generates reply tokens, which also count. When a long document is added and the total exceeds the limit, the oldest content is removed or replaced by a shorter summary. The narration then compares two outcomes: with an earlier detail still inside the window, the answer mentions it; after that detail falls out, the answer no longer uses it. The key message is that the model can only use what currently fits inside the token limit.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static sequence of five labelled panels replaces animation. Each panel shows the token bar at a different stage: empty, after instructions, after user text, after generated reply, and after overflow forces older content out or into a summary block.

workedExample.scenario: A reporting officer uses an approved assistant over several turns to revise talking points for a chief of section. The latest request adds a long background note and asks for a concise final version.
workedExample.input: Context limit: 1,000 tokens. System instructions: 120. Earlier conversation: 430. Latest request and background note: 380. Requested output: up to 200.
process: The full sequence would require up to 1,130 tokens, which exceeds the 1,000-token context window.
The application must reduce the input, allow less room for output or reject the request. In this example, it removes 130 tokens from the oldest conversation turn.
The model drafts the talking points using the remaining instructions, text and prior output. The removed passage is no longer available during generation.
A caveat found only in that passage does not appear in the draft, even though it was discussed earlier in the conversation.
workedExample.result: The talking points are fluent but omit the earlier caveat. Starting a fresh request with the essential instructions and source passages may produce a more reliable draft than relying on a long conversation history.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: At 5.20 pm, a statistician in a data unit asks an approved internal assistant to shorten a briefing note for a UN Country Team working group before the 6 pm deadline. The prompt includes drafting instructions, the current note, comments from several focal points and earlier exchanges with the assistant.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: All of that material, plus the text being generated, competes for space in the context window. If the combined sequence is too long, the application may reject the request, shorten the available output or remove earlier material. A qualification supplied near the start can therefore disappear from the model's usable context just when the final paragraph is drafted.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Use only material permitted in the approved tool. Personal, protection-sensitive, security-sensitive or other confidential information must not be pasted into a service that has not been approved for it. Check the draft against the source material, particularly where content may have been removed to fit the window.

whyItMatters: It affects whether a tool can handle long documents, long chats, and multi-step tasks without dropping important details. That matters for procurement, workflow design, risk assessment, and judging whether an output is complete enough to trust for review.
whereYouMayHearIt: A vendor demo during a procurement meeting
An ICT governance board reviewing an AI service
A data focal-point meeting on prompt guidance
A troubleshooting call with the service desk

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A larger context window means the model is smarter.
commonMisconceptions.correction: A larger window mainly means it can use more material at once. It may help with long inputs, but it does not automatically improve reasoning quality, factual reliability, or domain judgement.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Anything said earlier in a chat stays available forever.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Only the part that still fits in the current window is directly available unless the system stores and reinserts older content. Long conversations can therefore lose earlier details.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Context window and training data are the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Training happens before deployment and shapes the model weights. The context window is the temporary working input available during one interaction.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Memory limit means the model has human-like memory.
commonMisconceptions.correction: In this setting, memory limit usually refers loosely to the context limit. It does not mean the system forms durable personal memories unless extra memory features are added.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: It is the amount of recent text and instructions the model can look at at one time while answering.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: It is the model’s maximum usable sequence length for the current inference step, typically measured in tokens and shared across system prompt, user input, retrieved text, multimodal encodings where applicable, and generated output tokens.

keyTakeaway: The context window is the model's working limit for the current step. Instructions, source material, conversation history and generated output all use the same finite space.

quickCheck.question: What best explains why a chat assistant may ignore an important detail from much earlier in a long conversation?
options: The detail may have fallen outside the current context window.
The model deletes facts from its training data during long chats.
The vocabulary no longer contains the needed words.
quickCheck.explanation: The most likely reason is that the earlier detail no longer fits inside the current token limit available for this interaction. Training data, temperature, and vocabulary are different mechanisms.

issues.problem: The page treats “memory limit” as a looser synonym for context limit. That phrase is ambiguous and can easily be confused with the separate concept of long-term memory. Presenting it as the same idea undermines the distinction this page is required to maintain.
issues.fix: In plainExplanation, replace the final sentence of the first paragraph with: “Memory limit is ambiguous and should not be treated as a precise synonym.” Replace the correction in commonMisconceptions[3] with: “Memory limit is an ambiguous label. A context limit concerns material available during the current interaction. It does not mean the system forms durable personal memories unless extra memory features are added.”

issues.problem: The input total is correct: 120 + 80 + 260 + 300 = 760 tokens. The stated retention then uses the entire window: 120 + 80 + 300 + 100 of Paragraph A = 600. That leaves 600 - 600 = 0 tokens for the answer, contradicting the page’s technical statement that generated output shares the context limit. The example also asserts an unexplained truncation policy that favours Paragraph B.
issues.fix: Replace the process with: [“The instructions, question, and paragraphs total 760 tokens, so they do not all fit.”, “The tool is configured to reserve 100 tokens for the answer, leaving 500 input tokens.”, “It keeps the 200 tokens of instructions and question, plus 150 tokens from each paragraph.”, “The model generates up to 100 answer tokens from that retained text. An omitted qualification makes the comparison incomplete.”] This computes as 120 + 80 + 150 + 150 = 500 input tokens, then 500 + 100 = 600 total tokens.

issues.problem: The visual teaches that exceeding the limit causes the oldest content to be removed or summarised. That is not a general property of a context window. It is a tool-specific handling policy, and the model does not inherently choose that policy. The prose elsewhere correctly says behaviour depends on the tool.
issues.fix: Describe this as a configured simulation. In the description, write: “When proposed content exceeds the limit, the configured tool removes older content or replaces it with a summary.” In step 4, write: “In this simulation, the configured tool removes older material or replaces it with a shorter summary.” Make the same qualification in the accessibility description.

issues.problem: Option 0 is the only defensible answer. Option 1 is false because chats do not delete training data. Option 2 is false because temperature does not erase messages. Option 3 is false because vocabulary does not lose words during a chat. However, all three distractors are implausible mechanism claims, so the answer is obvious without understanding context windows or distinguishing the listed related terms.
issues.fix: Replace the quiz with: Question: “Which option defines a context window rather than a related term?” Options: [“The maximum amount of context usable at one time.”, “Stored information retrieved across separate sessions.”, “The process of adjusting a model using examples.”, “Repeating training examples instead of learning general rules.”] Keep correctOptionIndex as 0. Explanation: “Option 0 defines the context window. The other options describe long-term memory, training, and memorisation.”

issues.problem: Calling it an amount of “recent text” implies that recency determines what belongs in the window. A tool may retain instructions or selected material rather than simply the most recent text, and the context can include more than text.
issues.fix: It is the amount of current material and instructions the model can use at one time while answering.
